The first European settlers in Australia arrived in Port Phillip Bay around 1835. They established a settlement at Melbourne but found their efforts thwarted by the swamps and other natural obstacles along the coastline. After two years of hard work, they finally cleared enough land to build a small township, called Port Phillip. However, they soon realized that they needed something else besides just a few houses before they could establish themselves permanently.
In February 1836, Governor Lachlan Macquarie granted a large piece of Crown land south of Port Phillip Bay known as 'The Landing', near what later became Melbourne's city centre. He had been impressed with the success of the pioneers who had cleared land there and decided to make it an official port for the new colony. At the time, the largest ship in the world was the HMS Discovery, built in England, and she would need a deep harbour to accommodate her size. So the Governor ordered the construction of a wharf. By 1837, the first shipping lane into Port Phillip Bay opened up between Melbourne and Adelaide, South Australia.
By the end of 1838, 2,500 people lived in the newly formed capital city of Victoria. The population grew rapidly during the next decade, and within five years, Melbourne had become one of the most important cities in all of Australia.
As the population continued to grow, the need for more infrastructure increased. With no roads connecting the port with the rest of the country, the only way to transport goods was by water. And so began the construction of a system of dams, bridges, locks, and canals, which helped transform Victoria into a major trading hub.
This remarkable story of how one man, with nothing but his vision and determination, transformed an unknown region into a bustling metropolis continues today.

Input: Commercial turkeys are usually reared indoors under controlled conditions. These are often large buildings, purpose-built to provide ventilation and low light intensities (this reduces the birds' activity and thereby increases the rate of weight gain). The lights can be switched on for 24-hrs/day, or a range of step-wise light regimens to encourage the birds to feed often and therefore grow rapidly. Females achieve slaughter weight at about 15 weeks of age and males at about 19. Mature commercial birds may be twice as heavy as their wild counterparts. Many different breeds have been developed, but the majority of commercial birds are white, as this improves the appearance of the dressed carcass, the pin feathers being less visible. Turkeys were at one time mainly consumed on special occasions such as Christmas (10 million birds in the United Kingdom) or Thanksgiving (60 million birds in the United States). However, they are increasingly becoming part of the everyday diet in many parts of the world.
Output: What type of accomidations are domesticated turkey normally grown in?

outputs: In his book, The Cockpit, published in 1879, John Ruskin wrote, "The only good painting is that which is made by an artist who knows how not to paint". This was the title of a lecture he gave before the Royal Academy in London on October 1st, 1879. Ruskin's reputation rests largely upon these remarks; some believe them to be the most significant ever written against painting. He went on to say that there had never been a more perfect example than himself of what he meant by the word 'artist'. His work was known to have influenced the development of Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Cubism. It is said that Ruskin saw Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1898, when he was 83 years old.

Input: When learning how to write hanja, students are taught to memorize the native Korean pronunciation for the hanja's meaning and the Sino-Korean pronunciations (the pronunciation based on the Chinese pronunciation of the characters) for each hanja respectively so that students know what the syllable and meaning is for a particular hanja. For example, the name for the hanja 水 is 물 수 (mul-su) in which 물 (mul) is the native Korean pronunciation for "water", while 수 (su) is the Sino-Korean pronunciation of the character. The naming of hanja is similar to if "water" were named "water-aqua", "horse-equus", or "gold-aurum" based on a hybridization of both the English and the Latin names. Other examples include 사람 인 (saram-in) for 人 "person/people", 큰 대 (keun-dae) for 大 "big/large//great", 작을 소 (jakeul-so) for 小 "small/little", 아래 하 (arae-ha) for 下 "underneath/below/low", 아비 부 (abi-bu) for 父 "father", and 나라이름 한 (naraimreum-han) for 韓 "Han/Korea".
Output: What are students taught to memorize?

Its capital city Male is located on the island of Maafushi. The country has no natural harbor, so most trade must pass through the sea route known as the Strait of Malacca, connecting Malaysia to Sumatra. outputs: A man who could not speak to his own people would never understand them. But he had an audience to please, and that audience included himself. His name was Napoleon Bonaparte, and the story of his rise began when he was only 17 years old. He was born in Corsica, where his father was a wealthy landowner. After his mother died, his father married another woman, whose children became his stepchildren. When he reached adolescence, he was sent to France to study law. It was there that he met a young Frenchwoman named Josephine de Beauharnais. They fell deeply in love, and after Napoleon escaped to Italy, she followed him there. In Rome, he joined a political party, and soon found himself elected president of the Convention. At this point, the Revolutionary Wars broke out, and he saw action against the Austrians. With the help of his friend General Jean Baptiste Joubert, he defeated the Austrian army at Marengo. Although the victory was significant, Napoleon lost control of the war because he lacked the resources necessary to win battles. He also made enemies among the soldiers who fought under him. As Napoleon rose through the ranks, he became increasingly autocratic, and eventually, he seized power in Paris. Despite his initial successes, Napoleon ultimately faced defeat at Waterloo, losing the battle and much of Europe to the British.

Input:
outputs: The British Museum was founded in London in 1753 by royal charter issued under Queen Anne. Its first director was John Soane who had been made an architect to King George III. In his will he left all his property to the museum and the remainder to his wife Elizabeth so she could live there herself when they were old enough. He wanted his wife to take charge of the museum and her daughter Louisa would become his successor after his death. Despite having a reputation as a difficult man to work for, Soane was responsible for much of the building and decorative arts works in the museum during the early years of its existence. His design for the new building included two large galleries containing sculptures and paintings donated by the wealthiest families in Europe. He designed furniture for the collection and commissioned many artists to produce works for display in the museum. Among these artists were William Hogarth, whose portrait of Sir Joshua Reynolds painted for the British Museum became one of the most famous images of the time; and Jean-Antoine Watteau, known for his elegantly graceful landscapes. The museum also housed a collection of ancient Greek pottery, the oldest piece of which dates back to 8th century BC. It was moved to the museum in 1807 where it remains today. After Queen Victoria’s accession to the throne in 1837, the queen became patron of the museum and it grew considerably over the next few decades. During this period the collections expanded greatly through the acquisition of manuscripts, maps, prints and photographs. In addition, the museum began collecting contemporary artworks by some of the world’s leading artists, particularly French Impressionist painters. By the mid 19th century the museum had more than three million objects in its holdings. Today the British Museum has approximately four million items, making it the largest museum in the UK.

outputs: As part of our work on this year’s programme we were invited to join the Gathering at the RHS Wisley Flower Show, which took place on Saturday 23rd May 2016. We spent two days there visiting some fantastic displays, meeting wonderful people and learning lots of new things. In addition to seeing the amazing gardening skills demonstrated by many of the show’s designers, we also saw the ‘Rural Life’ section where you could find out how people live and work in rural Britain today. It was fascinating to see what was happening in farming and food production, the use of traditional crafts like basket making, blacksmithing and pottery, and much more besides. There are so many different aspects to this sector that it would take me a while to tell you everything I learned! What struck us most though was the number of people who had grown up around the countryside, often with a connection to animals or nature. They were passionate about keeping the land in good condition and working sustainably – something that really resonated with us too.

outputs: We’ve always known how much we love our dogs, but new research suggests that cats might also be emotional creatures. Overall, cats demonstrated higher levels of communication than most people realize. In fact, the researchers found that cats communicated more through nonverbal means than any other animal they studied, including chimpanzees, elephants, dolphins, and even horses.

Input: When learning how to write hanja, students are taught to memorize the native Korean pronunciation for the hanja's meaning and the Sino-Korean pronunciations (the pronunciation based on the Chinese pronunciation of the characters) for each hanja respectively so that students know what the syllable and meaning is for a particular hanja. For example, the name for the hanja 水 is 물 수 (mul-su) in which 물 (mul) is the native Korean pronunciation for "water", while 수 (su) is the Sino-Korean pronunciation of the character. The naming of hanja is similar to if "water" were named "water-aqua", "horse-equus", or "gold-aurum" based on a hybridization of both the English and the Latin names. Other examples include 사람 인 (saram-in) for 人 "person/people", 큰 대 (keun-dae) for 大 "big/large//great", 작을 소 (jakeul-so) for 小 "small/little", 아래 하 (arae-ha) for 下 "underneath/below/low", 아비 부 (abi-bu) for 父 "father", and 나라이름 한 (naraimreum-han) for 韓 "Han/Korea".
Output: What are students taught to memorize?

In a recent study, researchers found that when people look at images of faces, their brains activate regions associated with social cognition, including empathy and recognition. However, these brain responses differed depending on whether the image was familiar or novel.
In a study published this month in Nature Neuroscience, scientists used fMRI to examine how people process emotional stimuli in real time. They discovered that looking at an old photo caused significant activation in the amygdala, but only in response to pictures that were recently viewed. By contrast, when viewing a face, there was no significant difference between familiar and novel faces. These findings suggest that the brain has evolved to recognize recognizable facial features more quickly than less familiar ones.
The researchers also examined how long people looked at different types of faces before responding, finding that older adults had slower processing times compared to younger individuals. Older participants appeared to have a greater ability to identify the emotions conveyed through nonverbal cues, suggesting that this capacity may be linked to cognitive reserve. Overall, the study suggests that our visual system has adapted over time to better process social information, making us better able to interact with others in everyday life.
